THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Indo-European Languages: Steppes, Anatolia & the Hybrid Origin Debate

Stretching from Icelandic sagas and Welsh poetry to Persian ghazals and Sanskrit grammar before 1500 CE, the Indo-European family shares unmistakable regular cognates for kinship, wheels, yokes, and counting. Explaining how it spread bridges Bronze Age Yamnaya horse pastoralists with older Fertile Crescent farmers.

Reviews classical historical linguistics, cuneiform Hittite tablets, ancient Steppe genomes, and Heggarty et al. (2023) hybrid phylogenetic dates.

Anatolian, Steppe, and 2023 Hybrid Phylogenies

For decades scholars debated whether Indo-European spread outward from early Anatolian farmers (~8000 BP) or Bronze Age Yamnaya steppe herders (~5000 BP). Dense ancient DNA sampling proved both demographic pulses occurred sequentially across western Eurasia. [1] [2]

Heggarty et al. (2023) in Science proposed a hybrid synthesis from densely sampled core vocabulary trees (~8,100 BP root south of the Caucasus with later secondary steppe amplification into Europe and Central-South Asia), sparking lively integration with Steppe chariot and Tocharian Tarim archaeology. [1]

Written monuments from Mycenaean Linear B to Vedic hymns

Comparing Hittite cuneiform archives (c. 1650 BCE), Mycenaean Greek Linear B clay accounts (c. 1400 BCE), oral-transmitted Rigvedic Sanskrit, and Avestan hymns anchored the comparative method that established regular phonological laws across Eurasian branches. [1]

Maritime Latin–Romance, Slavic, and Indo-Iranian branches

Along Eurasia’s eastern and western extremes, Latin diversified into Mediterranean Romance languages while Middle Iranian (Sogdian, Persian), Indo-Aryan Prakrits, and Tocharian manuscripts along the Taklamakan rim documented Indo-European vitality deep across Inner and South Asia. [2] [3]
